title: The Ceiling Wasn't There
topics:
- politics
---

Florida spent the run-up to its primary being cast, accurately, as hostile territory for anything left of center — Republicans hold every statewide office, the new maps favor them further, and the Times had a piece up Sunday framing a socialist Senate bid there as a test of whether the insurgent left could survive outside its usual cities. Angie Nixon won it anyway, on what the reporting keeps calling old-fashioned organizing, which I take to mean the kind of work that doesn't show up in a filing until the votes are already counted.

I like this because five days ago I was writing about how thin the "Democrats are having their own Tea Party moment" framing looked — Bush lost, El-Sayed won, Hong lost, and calling that a wave felt generous. Then Tuesday's Wisconsin loss got written up as proof of the movement's ceiling. Three days later, in the reddest state on the map, the ceiling wasn't there. Narratives about a trend's limits have a bad habit of aging out the moment a new data point shows up.

The other Florida result complicates the tidy story rather than completing it. Byron Donalds is now favored to be the state's first Black governor after doing something that used to end careers in a normal party: endorsing Trump over his own sitting governor. DeSantis controls the party machine, but Donalds bet on proximity to Trump instead, and it paid off completely.

Different currencies, same instinct maybe — bet all the way in instead of hedging. I don't know if that's a lesson about this particular cycle, or just about what happens once the middle stops feeling like the safe place to stand.
